communications.subject: New York Freedom of Information Law Request: 2026 NFTA PD Flock Audit
communications.communication:
To Whom It May Concern:

Pursuant to the New York Freedom of Information Law, I hereby request the following records:

Records related to the NFTA Police Department’s Flock Safety system:
1. All contracts, licenses, MOUs, MOAs, data agreements, letters of intent, and other agreement documents with Flock Safety.
2. Organization Audit in Flock.
The report should include data logged from the period of January 1, 2020, to the date this request is processed. Per Flock's documentation, the Organization Audit is available within the Insights tab and is defined as searches done within the agency.

3. Network Audit in Flock.
The report should include data logged from the period of January 1, 2020, to the date this request is processed. Per Flock's documentation, the Network Audit is available within the Insights tab and is defined as searches of the organization’s Flock network by any agency in the Flock System.

4. A list of network share settings that include:
4a. Flock networks shared with the Department
4b. Networks that the Department is sharing

5. Flock Safety Event Log.
The report should include data logged from the period of January 1, 2020 to the date this request is processed. Per Flock's documentation, the Event Log is available within the Insights tab. Flock customer support may be able to assist with the mass-downloading of this data if assistance is required.

6. The locations and orientations of all ALPR cameras, including but not limited to Flock ALPR cameras, deployed by NFTA Transit PD


Records relating to the department's ALPR policy:
7. All versions of the applicable policies for the deployment of automated license plate recognition cameras/readers/systems, as well as for usage, storage and sharing of any data obtained by using such systems.

8. For the period January 1, 2020 to the date this request is processed: all records of periodic and/or random audits and inspections of ALPR use and ALPR data, including the audit reports themselves, findings, worksheets, spreadsheets, checklists, scoring rubrics, sampling methodology, and any corrective-action recommendations.

9. For the period January 1, 2020 to the date this request is processed: all records establishing the procedures and practices adopted to evaluate and monitor the use of LPR data and measure compliance of use with ALPR policy - including any standard operating procedure, audit protocol, directive, memorandum, or training bulletin describing how such audits are conducted, how often, and by whom.

10. All department communications (including email) concerning ALPR audits, inspections, compliance review, or policy violations written from the period of January 1, 2020 to the date this request is processed.

11. All records of any identified violations of department ALPR policy, including compliance notices, counseling memoranda, supervisory referrals, internal affairs complaints or investigations, findings, and any resulting discipline, concerning ALPR use or ALPR data.

12. All ALPR training records, including rosters, sign-in sheets, certificates, lesson plans, and curricula for ALPR training on (a) use of the technology, (b) the LPR policy and procedures, and (c) applicable laws and privacy protections; and any training bulletins issued.

13. The list of active authorized users with access to the ALPR system and records of additions to or removals from that list, from January 1, 2020 to the date this request is processed.

Please provide records in their original electronic, machine readable format. For example, please provide csv or spreadsheet files where applicable.

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter.

Sincerely,

Scott Conway

communications.subject: Illinois Freedom of Information Act. Request: Skokie Flock ALPR Emails 9-2026
communications.communication:
RE: Skokie Flock ALPR Emails 9-2026

To the FOIA Officer of Skokie Police Department,

This request is made under Illinois Freedom of Information Act. for the following records:

All emails and other written electronic correspondence sent to, received by, or copied ("cc'd" or "bcc'd") to any member of the Village of Skokie Board of Trustees (the Village President and all sitting Trustees, including Trustee Alison Pure Slovin) or to Village Manager John Lockerby, from January 1, 2026 through the date this request is processed, that reference, discuss, or relate to either of the following: "Flock" or "ALPR". Include any attachments to those emails.

For each responsive record, include the sender, all recipients (to/cc/bcc), date, and subject line in addition to the message body, so that correspondence can be attributed to the individual Trustee or the Village Manager who sent or received it. 

The requested documents will be made available to the general public, and this request is not being made for commercial purposes.

Fee estimates, if any apply, are requested in advance of fulfillment. Electronic delivery is the preferred method of receipt.

A response is anticipated within 5 business days, as the statute requires.

JB_𝗟𝗨𝗖𝗬 𝝦𝝙𝝘𝗦𝝝𝝥𝗦 𝗟𝝙𝝗𝗦

--
BACKGROUND

At the Village of Skokie Board of Trustees meeting on September 8, 2026 (video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RjmNFg15eww), Trustee Alison Pure Slovin (District 2) told the Board that unlike her colleagues, several of whom described hearing concerns from residents about the Village's Flock automated license plate reader (ALPR) program, she had heard privately from constituents in her district who support the Flock cameras. In her words, as recorded in the meeting:

> "...we keep talking about the residents who've reached out to numerous trustees on this board. I'm concerned about these Flock cameras, as everybody said. But I can't speak for the other trustees. But I could tell you that people within the district that I serve, so to speak, have also reached out to me maybe privately and not to all the trustees and have said that they support it because they feel that there is a safety issue and anything that Skokie can do to keep them safe is something that they would commend us on and to continue with. So, you know, we're talking about the few that have reached out to us, but there are the others who are reaching out to us as well. And we have to balance both voices on this board as we move forward. And then if we talk about the amount of people who have reached out to us against Flock cameras, I can't speak for everybody else. It's a dozen people I've heard from. It's not like hundreds of people either. So, you know, we have to really look at who we're representing, what the needs are of this community, and how we help you keep them safe. And the recommendations are from the professionals, and I thank you for that."

Trustee Pure Slovin's comments came during the same September 8, 2026 meeting where the Skokie Police presented on its use of Flock Group ("Flock Safety") automated license plate readers (ALPR), and where numerous Skokie community members spoke during public comment against the Village's Flock ALPR camera network. 

Before public comment began, the board president instituted new decorum rules for the meeting, barring "clapping," "snapping," "standing," or "audible cheers," cast as necessary so that "all positions and voices can be expressed and heard without fear of reprisal." That public comment period then filled to its allotted capacity, roughly ten speakers at three minutes each, and with one exception unrelated to Flock (a labor dispute at a local bakery), every speaker who addressed the Village's Flock/ALPR program spoke against it. No speaker voiced support for Flock or ALPR on the record that night; the only support referenced anywhere in the meeting is the private, secondhand support Trustee Pure Slovin described above. Some quotes from that public comment period:

- "Flock is not an honest company," one commenter said, citing recent contract cancellations in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, and on state-run roads in Texas and Florida: "When I am on the same side as Ron DeSantis, I am embarrassed."
- Another commenter asked how the Village squares its own inclusion and belonging campaigns with "an atmosphere of distrust and fear that is created by flock cameras."
- A third commenter, working through a hypothetical involving a lawful firearm purchase, argued that Flock's camera network could function as a "de facto registry," with every Flock-equipped municipality along a driver's route adding to the trail.
- A commenter who worked through the Skokie Police Department's own case data noted that two of the resulting arrests were for cannabis in an improperly sealed container, not impaired driving, and asked whether those stops would have happened at all without "a false flag in the system."
- A commenter whose work involves information security argued "we can solve crimes without tracking everyone in public," and noted that Flock data collected in Skokie has already been reachable by outside agencies working around Illinois' restrictions on data sharing.
- A commenter affiliated with Lucy Parsons Labs and the Niles Coalition told the Board that the Skokie Police Department's Flock ALPR program has drawn scrutiny as part of "years of work by a coalition of researchers right here in Illinois," documented in a zine published at nilescoalition.org.
- A commenter warned that Flock's AI-enabled search tools mean "you don't really need facial recognition" to identify someone, since the system can be told to find a person matching a plain-language description and "bring in a live feed of that person as they're walking by."
- Another commenter said "there's just no reality on earth that comes to my mind that doesn't make this feel like an Orson Wells novel," adding that discussing "the idea of us living in a surveillance state" with the Board, over cameras that would also watch their own children, was hard to believe.
- A final commenter asked the Board directly how Flock can share footage with law enforcement on request when a homeowner's doorbell-camera network cannot do the same without a subpoena or the owner's consent.

The Lucy Parsons Labs/Niles Coalition commenter also said they had emailed the Board roughly six months earlier, in or around March 2026, with findings on the Skokie Police Department's use of ethnic slurs and its suppression of public ALPR audit logs, and that "nobody has followed up." That unanswered correspondence is part of why this request is being made: it, and any Trustee discussion or response it prompted, should fall within the scope of the records sought above.

During Board discussion of the Flock program, a Trustee referenced haveibeenflocked.com, a third-party tool that lets residents check whether their own license plate data has been captured by Flock cameras, as a resource that could help residents understand the program.

Skokie is one of many Chicago-area and Illinois municipalities where Flock automated license plate reader cameras (also called ALPR or license plate reader cameras) have become a point of public debate, alongside neighboring communities such as Evanston, Lincolnwood, Morton Grove, Wilmette, Winnetka, and Highland Park, and amid a broader statewide and national reckoning with the weapons technology tracked by organizations like Lucy Parsons Labs, the Niles Coalition, and the crowdsourced camera-mapping project DeFlock.org. The only reason Skokie PD, as with those across the country, started taking performative technological reforms was though diligent work by activists. That reckoning though has not slowed Skokie's own program: the Village's Flock cameras were already active by 2023 and remain in place through September 2026, notwithstanding the near-unanimous opposition voiced at the meeting described above. This request is part of an ongoing effort to obtain public records documenting how Flock Group ALPR surveillance technology is adopted and defended by outposts of empire like the Village of Skokie.
